Hi, I've always wanted to know what skip traces are. I had a friend who I gave rides to work when he worked for a debt collection agency, and the receptionist basically answered the phone all day and told people that they didn't do that.

Skipping someone can involve a lot of different things.

Most commonly, it involves pulling a person's Credit Bureau Report and looking at it. The information on that report comes, for the most part, from you. If you filled out an apartment application, you gave them your phone number, your address, your place of employment, etc. Same when you applied for cellphone service, a credit card, or whatever else. So now, if I look at your CBR, I have that information. Then I try to call you and get you to make some plans to pay your debt.

Also common are a couple of things that are really similar to a CBR, but aren't CBR's. Accurint is the name of the most common one. Accurint's advantage is that it can tell me your phone number and address, your dad's phone and address, your neighbor's number, other phone numbers that are at the address you live at but not in your name (sister, roommate, etc.)

Maybe you've listed "references" on a credit app at some point; probably your mom and another relative. I can call your mom or whoever. I cannot tell them that you owe a debt, but I can pump them for information about how to get ahold of you. If is so happens that either (a) they get mad that I asked so many questions or (b) they think you're in legal trouble, then maybe momma calls you and reams you out. If that leads to you paying, then hooray!

I can also try to find information about you on Google or LinkedIn or whatever. If you have an unusual name, or a common name but live in a small town, it's pretty easy to find out where you work.

Skipping is about half the job. Once you have them on the phone, convincing them that it's time to pay now is the other half of the job.

How: With a telephone, silly!

At what percentage of the face value do you buy the debt for?

The answer to that question a couple management-tiers above me on the pay grade, but I know that it can vary widely. They're bought in batches, not one-by-one.

Maybe Batch A has an average debtor aged 27, with an average credit score of 650, primarily in Colorado. It will be worth more than Batch B, which has an average debtor age of 68, with an average credit score of 570, located primarily in West Virginia. This is because batch A are mostly working age in an affluent state, which batch B are mostly SSDI age in a poor state.

As to the actual percentage, it can vary from 10% to 100% of the face value of the debts. I know a lot of people get mad when the collection agency won't knock 80% off their debt, because it was bought for "pennies on the dollar."

If you happen to have a good credit score, live in a wealthier state, and the debt is relatively recent, then there is every chance that the collection agency bought it for 80 pennies on the dollar, or more.
